entries.clue: Leader of Beatles and Wings? (4)

indicatorNotes.Leader of: The leader of a word is the letter at its head, so that single opening letter is all that is taken.

blocks.note: the letter the name begins on
the clue's own little word, spelling itself out

annotation.surface: A question about who fronted two famous groups.
annotation.walkthrough: Paul McCartney is the man the surface points at: he was in the Beatles and then started the other group named here. The question mark admits that group is one example of the answer rather than a synonym for it.
annotation.definitionFit: Wings was the group Paul McCartney formed in 1971, so the definition names the answer by one instance of it.

entries.clue: Managing to set peg in gearwheel (6)

indicatorNotes.set: To set a thing is to fix it into place in something else, which is the instruction to bury one word in another.
indicatorNotes.in: 'In' names the destination: what comes before it ends up inside what comes after.

blocks.note: a cog is the toothed wheel in a gear train
a pin is the small peg that holds two parts together

annotation.surface: A machine being repaired by fixing a peg into one of its gearwheels.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Managing' in the surface is running something; the answer takes the humbler sense of getting by. The peg and the gearwheel belong to one machine, so nothing in the picture warns you that one word has to go inside the other.
annotation.definitionFit: To cope is to manage — to get through what is in front of you — and both words are in the -ing form.

entries.clue: It stops water: a minute monster (10)

blocks.note: the cock on a pipe is the tap that shuts the flow off, as in stopcock
the article, taken as it stands
a trice is a moment, which is what a minute means when it is loosely a short time

annotation.surface: A tap, described as though it were a very small beast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Minute' is the trap: the surface wants the tiny sense, said my-NOOT, and the wordplay wants the unit of time in its loose sense of a moment. The creature itself is heraldry's cock-headed serpent, hatched from a cock's egg.
annotation.definitionFit: A cockatrice is the mythical serpent with a cockerel's head that was said to kill with a look, so 'monster' names it by its kind.

entries.clue: Halfway to catching bad end, paid attention (6)

indicatorNotes.catching: What is caught is held inside the thing that catches it, so one piece closes round the other.
indicatorNotes.bad: A bad copy of a word has its letters out of true, so they are to be set down in another order.

blocks.note: mid is the word for halfway along something
the three letters of the word beside it, reordered before they go in

annotation.surface: Someone well on the way to a bad end who finally started taking notice.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bad end' looks like the familiar instruction to take the last letter of a word, and that reading gets you one letter and no further. 'Bad' is the shuffler here, and 'end' is the three letters shuffled.
annotation.definitionFit: To mind something is to attend to it — mind the gap — so the past form matches 'paid attention' exactly.

entries.clue: Red light flickering on panel across motorway (4,4)

indicatorNotes.flickering: A flickering light will not hold still, and letters that will not hold still have to be set down in another order.
indicatorNotes.across: Something lying across a thing has parts to either side of it, so the shuffled letters close round the one named next.

blocks.note: seven letters to be reordered
M is the letter Britain numbers its motorways with — the M1, the M25

annotation.surface: A warning light blinking on a gantry panel above the motorway.
annotation.walkthrough: Neon's own glow is orange-red, so the definition is what the thing literally looks like rather than a piece of misdirection. Only one letter comes from outside the shuffled phrase, and 'across' is what puts it in the middle.
annotation.definitionFit: A neon tube glows orange-red when current runs through it, which makes it a red light in the plainest sense.

entries.clue: Boatman will, you say, be here, surrounded by the sea (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a description rather than a noun: it points at a place with water on every side instead of naming it, which is what lets the setter put himself in the sentence.

indicatorNotes.you say: What you say is the sound of a word, so what is wanted is something said the same way and spelt differently.

blocks.note: Boatman is this setter's pen name, so the setter saying what he will do is 'I'll', and that contraction said aloud is what you write
the verb the surface needs to make a sentence of itself; it adds nothing to the letters

annotation.surface: The setter promising to be waiting for you somewhere with water all round it.
annotation.walkthrough: The first person in a crossword is always the setter, and here he is named outright, which is the only way the contraction can be reached. Boatman has signed Guardian puzzles under that name since 2009.
annotation.definitionFit: An isle is a small island, which is exactly a piece of land with the sea all the way round it.

entries.clue: Confetti: romantic, unusual after discontented multitudes contacted this way (8)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a description rather than a synonym: it says how the crowd was reached, and the noun names the sheet they were reached by.

indicatorNotes.discontented: Contents are what sits inside, so a word robbed of them keeps only the letters at its two ends.

blocks.note: the C it opens on and the I it closes on
the same treatment: the R at the front, the C at the back
the U and the L at its two ends
the A and the R that bookend it, and the word is fodder rather than joinery

annotation.surface: Confetti called romantic but odd, thrown after unhappy crowds had been given the news.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Discontented' sits next to the multitudes and reads as their mood; it is in fact pointing backwards at the four words before it, each of which loses its middle. One indicator doing four jobs is why the wordplay looks like a list.
annotation.definitionFit: A circular is the printed sheet a firm or a council posts to everyone on its list at once, which is how a multitude gets contacted.

entries.clue: Thong placing little weight on top of thigh (4)

indicatorNotes.placing: The clue is telling you where to put things, so the two pieces are set down one against the other.
indicatorNotes.on: In a down entry what is placed on something sits above it, so the short piece is written first.

blocks.note: w is the standard abbreviation for weight, and 'little' asks for the short form
the hip is the joint sitting at the top of the thigh

annotation.surface: A skimpy garment that weighs almost nothing where it sits on the leg.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Thong' is the trap: the sentence has it as underwear, and the answer takes the older sense, a narrow strip of hide. 'Top of thigh' looks like an instruction to take a first letter and is anatomy instead.
annotation.definitionFit: A thong is a strip of leather, and the lash of the answer is exactly that — the sense the word still has in the saddler's trade.

entries.clue: One cool about cut-down tree to show regret (9)

indicatorNotes.about: To go about a thing is to pass round it, so the word before opens up and takes the word after inside.

blocks.note: one = a, the indefinite article
poise is coolness, the self-possession of someone unruffled
a tree that has been felled and trimmed is a log

annotation.surface: A calm person saying sorry about a tree that has come down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cool' wants to be a temperature or an attitude and is the noun for composure. The tree is wanted as the timber it becomes once it is down, not as the act of felling it.
annotation.definitionFit: To apologise is to say you are sorry out loud, which is showing regret rather than merely feeling it.

entries.clue: Forger correcting mismatch without using Mac? (5)

indicatorNotes.correcting: Correcting something puts right what is in the wrong place, so the letters are to be reordered.
indicatorNotes.without using: What is not used is left out, so those letters are struck from the ones they were sitting in.

blocks.note: the eight letters to work on
the three letters that come out of them, in the surface an Apple computer

annotation.surface: Somebody fixing a mismatch on a computer that is not an Apple.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Forger' has nothing to do with fakes: a smith forges iron at an anvil, and the word for the criminal came later from the same image. The mismatch is corrected by moving its letters, once three of them have gone.
annotation.definitionFit: A smith works metal at a forge, so 'forger' is the literal job description rather than the criminal one.

entries.clue: At last melted ice to make liquid (5)

indicatorNotes.At last: At last means at the very end, so only the final letter of the word beside it is taken.

blocks.note: the letter it finishes on
the sheet of ice you skate on is a rink

annotation.surface: Ice that has finally melted into a puddle.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing in the picture hints that the ice is a place rather than the stuff, which is where the four letters come from. 'At last' reads as an impatient adverb and is an instruction pointing at the word next to it.
annotation.definitionFit: A drink is liquid taken by mouth, so the noun stands in for the answer directly, if rather more generally.

entries.clue: Clue to depth: symbolically, the mark of a fool (6,3)

annotation.definition: Clue to depth: symbolically, the mark of a fool

blocks.note: read as a hint about how deep something is, and meant as the letter that stands for depth on a drawing — the one the answer's first word wears at its top
read as any sign of foolishness, and meant as the pointed paper hat a slow pupil was stood in the corner wearing

annotation.surface: A hint about measuring depth that turns into an insult.
annotation.walkthrough: D is the symbol for depth on a plan or a dimension label. The joke is that the answer describes itself: the cap of its first word is that very letter, so the thing named is also the clue to it.
annotation.definitionFit: A dunce's cap is the conical paper hat a child was made to wear at the front of the class, the traditional sign that someone has been judged stupid.

entries.clue: Saw rowing crews swapping sides before end of pond (7)

indicatorNotes.swapping sides: Swapping sides means the letters at the two ends change places, each taking the position the other had.
indicatorNotes.before: Before fixes the running order: what it introduces is written first.
indicatorNotes.end of: The end of a word is the letter it stops on, and that one letter is all that is wanted.

blocks.note: an eight is a racing boat rowed by eight oarsmen, and the crew takes the boat's name
the letter it finishes on

annotation.surface: Rowing crews changing banks just short of the end of the lake.
annotation.walkthrough: The sides being swapped are the letters at the two ends of the crews' word, not the banks of the water the surface puts them on. Only two letters move, which is what makes this feel less like a shuffle than it is.
annotation.definitionFit: To have sighted something is to have caught sight of it, and the past tense matches 'saw' exactly.

entries.clue: Animals moving to sierra from top of forest where it’s hot (5)

indicatorNotes.moving to: Moving to a new letter means the old one gives up its place and the newcomer stands there instead.
indicatorNotes.from: 'From' names what is being left behind — the letter that has to go.
indicatorNotes.top of: The top of a word, read down the grid, is the letter it begins with.

blocks.note: the fauna of a place is the animal life living in it
sierra is S in the radio spelling alphabet
the letter the word begins with, and the one the newcomer pushes out

annotation.surface: Wildlife leaving the top of the forest for the mountains, where the heat is.
annotation.walkthrough: Sierra is the radio alphabet's S rather than a mountain range, and 'top of forest' is the letter the word starts with rather than a spot on the hillside. Both readings are in the surface's landscape, which is what hides them.
annotation.definitionFit: A sauna is the Finnish steam bath, a room kept deliberately hot, so the definition names it by the one thing it is for.

entries.clue: Heavenly confection of glacé nuts and ices, principally (7)

indicatorNotes.confection of: A confection is put together out of whatever is to hand, so the letters are assembled in a new order.
indicatorNotes.principally: What is principal comes first, so each word named gives up only the letter at its head.

blocks.note: five letters; the accent on the e is no part of the spelling in the grid
the first letter of the word
and the first letter of this one

annotation.surface: A pudding of candied fruit, nuts and ice cream, called divine.
annotation.walkthrough: Glacé fruit is fruit candied in syrup, which is why the word is in a dessert at all. 'Principally' reaches over both 'nuts' and 'ices' but not over 'and', which is doing nothing but joining them.
annotation.definitionFit: Angelic means of or like an angel, and heavenly carries that same sense of belonging to the skies rather than merely being delightful.

entries.clue: Seeing prejudice toward men’s side, anger erupts around Britain (6,4)

annotation.definitionNote: Gender bias runs either way, and leaning toward men is one instance of it, so the setter is defining the whole thing by its commonest example.

indicatorNotes.erupts: What erupts is thrown out and lands anyhow, so the letters come down in a new order.
indicatorNotes.around: Going around a thing means passing either side of it, so the letter named stays inside the rest.

blocks.note: four of the letters to be reordered, borrowed from the phrase about men
five more
B is the usual single letter for Britain
the surface's opening, setting up what the anger is a reaction to; it carries no letters

annotation.surface: Anger breaking out across the country at unfair treatment of the men's team.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Side' looks like the last word of the phrase about men and is fodder instead, which is what makes the join so hard to find. B for Britain is dropped into the middle of the shuffle rather than added to either end.
annotation.definitionFit: Gender bias is prejudice shown for or against people because of their sex, and favouring men is one direction that takes.

entries.clue: Part of dance, popular for group (5)

blocks.note: the cha-cha is a Latin ballroom dance, and this is half of its name
in = popular, in the sense of being in fashion

annotation.surface: A dance step that has caught on with a crowd.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Part of dance' is asking for part of a dance's name, not a step in one: the cha-cha gives up its first half. The definition is the commercial sense — a set of shops or hotels run by one owner.
annotation.definitionFit: A chain is a set of shops or hotels trading under one owner, so 'group' is the word the business pages would use for it.

entries.clue: It tastes distinctively yummy, even with a half of mild (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a sentence about the answer rather than a synonym for it: the answer is a noun naming the savoury taste that stands apart from sweet, sour, salt and bitter.

indicatorNotes.even: Even means the evenly numbered letters — the second, the fourth — with the odd ones passed over.
indicatorNotes.half of: Half of a four-letter word is two letters, and it is the opening pair that joins on to what has gone before.

blocks.note: its second and fourth letters, taken in order
the article, spelling itself
half the word, the first two of its four letters

annotation.surface: A distinctly delicious taste, helped along by half a pint of mild.
annotation.walkthrough: Mild is a dark, lightly hopped British beer, so 'a half of mild' is an order at the bar as well as two letters out of four. 'Even' counts positions in a word; nothing in the picture is even.
annotation.definitionFit: Umami is the savoury fifth taste, the one stock, soy sauce and parmesan carry, recognised alongside sweet, sour, salt and bitter.

entries.clue: Saw crash or mishap (8)

indicatorNotes.crash: A crash leaves what it hits in pieces, and the pieces of a word are its letters in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: eight letters to be reordered, the little word among them counting as fodder

annotation.surface: An accident on the road, described two ways over.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Saw' reads as the past tense of see in a sentence about a crash, and it is the noun for an old saying — 'more haste, less speed' is a saw. 'Or' belongs to the letters, not to the joinery.
annotation.definitionFit: An aphorism is a terse general truth, which is what an old saw is: the plain English word for the same thing.

entries.clue: Tear often expressed in epitaph (3)

blocks.note: the verb for pulling cloth or paper apart, and the noun for the split it leaves
the three letters carved at the foot of a headstone, short for rest in peace

annotation.surface: Grief put into the wording on a gravestone.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface wants the teardrop and the wordplay wants the one in the cloth — same spelling, different sound, which is why the first word reads so innocently. The letters on the stone are short for the Latin requiescat in pace.
annotation.definitionFit: To rip is to tear, the same action in the same part of speech, and the letters are also the ones cut into a headstone to wish the dead rest.

entries.clue: Part of trivium occultum in myrrh et orichalco? (8)

indicatorNotes.occultum in: Occultum is Latin for concealed, so the letters are already sitting in an unbroken row inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: the run starts partway through the first word and stops partway through the last, crossing both gaps without a break

annotation.surface: A scrap of Latin about myrrh and a legendary metal.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics are the tell that the tail of the clue is Latin: orichalcum is the lost metal of Atlantis, and the phrase says 'concealed in myrrh and orichalcum'. The trivium was the first three of the seven liberal arts taught in medieval schools.
annotation.definitionFit: The trivium is grammar, logic and rhetoric, the medieval curriculum's first three arts, so the definition names the answer as one of that set.

entries.clue: Girl cycling round country house (5)

indicatorNotes.cycling round: Letters cycling round travel off the front of the word and back on at the end, one at a time, never changing their order.

blocks.note: a manor is the principal house of a country estate

annotation.surface: A girl riding her bike round a big house in the country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' is a bicycle on the surface and a letter-wheel underneath, and two letters have to make the trip, not one. Norma is a woman's name and also Bellini's opera about a druid priestess.
annotation.definitionFit: Crosswords use 'girl' to mean any woman's first name, and Norma is one — the relation is naming by class, not synonymy.

entries.clue: Primarily, anyone trying hurdles, lifting, endurance training etc (7)

annotation.definition: Primarily, anyone trying hurdles, lifting, endurance training etc

indicatorNotes.Primarily: What comes primarily comes first, so every word in the list that follows gives up its opening letter.

blocks.note: the first letter of the list's first word
the next word's opening letter
the letter the first of the events named begins with
the opening letter of the weightlifter's word
the letter this one starts with
the first letter of the word for the work behind them all
even the abbreviation at the end has a first letter, and it is wanted

annotation.surface: A list of the events and sessions somebody has taken on.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word does two jobs at once: it describes what the answer does and hands over its opening letter, so no word is left to act as a separate definition. 'Etc' is fodder too, which is where the trick hides.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes someone who trains and competes at running, jumping and lifting — the whole sentence is the definition.

entries.clue: Drop price of bundle, cutting $0.0075 (7)

indicatorNotes.cutting: To cut into something is to go inside it, so the money named next is split open to take the other word in.

blocks.note: three quarters of a cent, and three quarters of the coin's four letters, the last one dropped
a heap of something is a bundle of it

annotation.surface: Knocking three quarters of a cent off the price of a bundle.
annotation.walkthrough: The arithmetic is the joke: 0.0075 of a dollar is three quarters of a cent, and taking three quarters of the word is what the figure is really asking for. The dollar sign is what tells you which coin.
annotation.definitionFit: To cheapen something is to bring its price down, which is what a shop does when it marks stock down.

entries.clue: Perhaps saw Boatman’s craft (6)

blocks.note: a tool that cuts, of which a saw is one sort — hence the 'perhaps'
a small single-masted sailing boat, and Boatman is this setter's own pen name

annotation.surface: Someone thinking they caught sight of the setter's boat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps saw' reads as a half-remembered glimpse and is the toolshed instead. The setter's name makes the second half personal: his craft is both the boat and, by a pun the puzzle keeps returning to, the trade of clue-writing.
annotation.definitionFit: A cutter is anything that cuts, a saw among them, and a cutter is also a light single-masted vessel — two unconnected senses of one word.

entries.clue: Controversially doping chimp? (6)

indicatorNotes.Controversially: Something controversial is disputed and unsettled, so the letters will not stay in the order they are given.

blocks.note: six letters to be reordered

annotation.surface: An accusation that somebody has been giving drugs to a chimpanzee.
annotation.walkthrough: The word is the zoologist's, from the Pongidae, the family of the great apes. The question mark is doing real work: one ape is standing in for the whole family.
annotation.definitionFit: A pongid is a member of the great-ape family, so a chimpanzee is one instance of the answer rather than a synonym for it.

entries.clue: Tough interviewer of disgraced president could show what’s generally evident in Greenland (4,5)

blocks.note: hard = tough, of a person or of a question
David Frost, the British broadcaster, interviewed Richard Nixon in 1977, three years after Watergate drove him from office

annotation.surface: A famously unyielding interviewer putting his questions to a president who left in disgrace.
annotation.walkthrough: The Frost–Nixon interviews became a play and then a film, which is how the pairing stays familiar. The definition is a picture rather than a synonym: Greenland's ground is frozen solid for most of the year.
annotation.definitionFit: A hard frost is a freeze severe enough to stiffen the ground, which is the ordinary state of Greenland outside high summer.

entries.clue: Journalist’s unauthorised access (4)

blocks.note: Fleet Street's own word for a jobbing reporter, more rueful than rude
getting into a computer or a phone account without permission

annotation.surface: A reporter getting into records he has no right to see.
annotation.walkthrough: Both senses met in the phone-hacking scandal that closed the News of the World, which is why the two halves read as one phrase. The journalist sense is much older: a hack was a hired drudge, from the hackney horse let out by the hour.
annotation.definitionFit: A hack is a jobbing journalist, and a hack is also a break-in to a computer system — the same four letters in two unconnected trades.

entries.clue: Worry reflecting one taking part in the culture wars (4)

indicatorNotes.reflecting: A reflection shows a thing the other way round, so the letters are read back from the far end.

blocks.clueFragment: one taking part in the culture wars
blocks.note: TERF is the acronym for a trans-exclusionary radical feminist, a label coined in the arguments over gender

annotation.surface: Anxiety mirroring the state of someone caught up in the arguments of the day.
annotation.walkthrough: The culture wars are Britain's running public arguments over identity and language, and the four letters turned round are the acronym for one side of the gender row. 'Reflecting' is safe in a down clue because a mirror has no preferred axis.
annotation.definitionFit: To fret is to worry — to gnaw away at something in your mind — and both words are the verb.

entries.clue: Maybe settle in Switzerland, behind a mountain (5)

indicatorNotes.behind: Behind a thing is after it, so the piece named first in the clue is the one that ends up second.

blocks.note: a ben is a Scottish mountain — Ben Nevis is the highest of them
CH is Switzerland's international code, from Confoederatio Helvetica, the Latin name on its car plates

annotation.surface: Somebody thinking of making a home in Switzerland, under a mountain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Settle' reads as making a home abroad and is a piece of furniture underneath. Ben is Gaelic for a peak, which is why so many Scottish hills are Ben something.
annotation.definitionFit: A settle is a long wooden seat with a high back and arms, one particular kind of bench, and 'maybe' admits it is only an example.

entries.clue: Help remove packaging from fizzy beverage (4)

indicatorNotes.remove packaging from: Packaging is the wrapping a thing arrives in, so the letters on the outside of the word come away.

blocks.note: shandy is beer topped up with lemonade, the half-pint a British pub pours for the driver

annotation.surface: Getting the wrapping off a fizzy drink.
annotation.walkthrough: The wrapping that comes off is a single letter at each end, not a word round the outside, which is the step most solvers try first. Shandy is a long-standing British bar order rather than a brand.
annotation.definitionFit: To give someone a hand is to help them, so the noun stands in for help in the everyday idiom.

entries.clue: Class division: a problem to be investigated, taking time (5)

indicatorNotes.taking: A word that takes something in opens up and makes room for it inside itself.

blocks.note: a case is the matter a detective or a lawyer takes on
t is the standard abbreviation for time

annotation.surface: An unsolved problem that needs looking into and will take a while.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Taking time' reads as the investigation dragging on and is the instruction to bury a single letter. The word itself is Portuguese, from casta, meaning lineage, and the traders carried it to India.
annotation.definitionFit: A caste is one of the hereditary ranks a society is split into, so 'class division' names both the rank and the split that makes it.

entries.clue: Laa-Laa etc skipping every repeat (9)

indicatorNotes.skipping: What you skip you leave out, so the letters named next are missing from the word they were sitting in.

blocks.note: a name that repeats its own opening sound is an example of alliteration, and 'etc' widens it from the one name to the device
every = all, the three letters that go

annotation.surface: A children's television name and the others like it, with the repeats left out.
annotation.walkthrough: Laa-Laa is one of the Teletubbies, and the name repeats its own opening sound, which is what alliteration is. 'Every' looks like a quantifier attached to 'repeat' and is the word being skipped.
annotation.definitionFit: An iteration is one more go round of the same thing, which is what a repeat is — the noun rather than the verb.
